What is different about selling inside Metro Nashville's single government?

Since 1963 the city and Davidson County have run as one Metro government, which puts valuation, billing and deed recording for a sale under one roof. Only Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville levy a separate city tax of their own. Terrain matters too: the Cumberland River cuts through the Nashville Basin while the Highland Rim hills ring the west, so listings often mention slopes and retaining walls.

Census Bureau figures for mid-2025 show 721,074 residents in the Nashville-Davidson balance, a 4.6% rise over the 2020 base. Owners occupy just 52.4% of homes, so landlords, heirs and people changing jobs make up a big slice of sellers. Use the table to see which Metro desk answers which question.

What does Census data reveal about housing in Nashville?

For 2020 to 2024, QuickFacts shows a median owner-occupied value of $413,600 and a median rent of $1,586. There are 313,513 households here, averaging 2.13 people, and 80.7% of residents stayed put over the previous year.

  • Median household income: $77,371 in 2024 dollars
  • College graduates, 25 and older: 48.0%
  • Average commute: 24.7 minutes each way
  • Share of people in poverty: 14.1%

Averages hide a lot. A downtown condo and a ranch house in Antioch sit far apart, so study comparable sales near your address before choosing a price. The figures come from Census QuickFacts.

Why did Nashville tax bills jump after the 2025 reappraisal?

Values were mailed on April 18, 2025 and the median parcel rose 45%, with council district medians running from 38% to 54%. The state first trimmed the old rates to revenue-neutral levels, according to the Assessor, and then Metro raised them again: owners in the Urban Services District pay $2.814 for each $100 assessed, and those in the General Services District pay $2.782. Those are jumps of 26% and 39% over the certified rates. Only the value is open to appeal.

State law taxes a house on 25% of its appraised value. Run the Census median of $413,600 through that and the taxable amount is about $103,400, and the Trustee's method yields roughly $2,909 in the Urban Services District or $2,876 elsewhere in the county. The 2025 windows, May 9 for informal reviews and June 27 for formal appeals, have closed. For future cycles, ask the Assessor's appraisal staff at 615-862-6059.

What will the Trustee's bill look like when I close?

The Trustee prints the annual statement for the parcel's owner of record, and it covers the whole calendar year. Your title company should divide it on the settlement sheet. Unpaid amounts follow the parcel, so confirm that the year is settled before you hand over keys.

  • Statements go out in early October, and the first Monday of October is the due date.
  • Interest-free payment runs to the end of February.
  • From March 1 the Trustee adds 1.5% per month.
  • A card payment adds 2.55% (minimum $2.00); an e-check adds $1.00.

No Tennessee rule obliges the Trustee to mail a notice, so a lost bill does not pause interest. Parcels that stay delinquent go to a tax sale auction, with a one-year redemption right for the owner.

Does Nashville offer property tax relief that a seller should mention?

For owners 65 and up there is a freeze, and low-income elderly or disabled owners and disabled veterans can claim relief. The Comptroller's 2026 table caps freeze income at $54,900 here. A veteran rated 100% disabled has no income test, and the relief applies to the first $175,000 of market value.

Mention any of these to the buyer's side early, so the settlement figures reflect the real bill. The Trustee's office at 615-862-6330 can say which proofs of age, residence and income it wants.

What happens at the Register of Deeds on Deaderick Street?

The office at 300 Deaderick Street files deeds and also accepts remote filings. The state adds 37 cents for every $100 of price on the transfer. It takes original documents with notarized signatures, and its staff cannot draft a deed or search for liens. Hire a title company or attorney for that.

Anyone can search the indexes in the office, and online access is sold by subscription. Ask the closer to record on the day you sign so the new deed is indexed quickly, and request a certified copy later if you need one for your files.

Does a short term rental permit stay with a Nashville house?

It does not. Metro Codes ties the permit to a named holder and one address, and any change of owner cancels it, including a move from a person into a trust or LLC. Anyone wanting nightly guests must file from scratch.

  • A permit lapses 365 days after issue unless renewed.
  • The guest count tops out at twice the sleeping rooms plus four, never more than 12.
  • Renters must be 21 or older.
  • Three code violations can cost the holder the permit.

Put the permit status in your offer paperwork. The Metro Codes operating rules spell out every condition.

What is the story behind Nashville's older neighborhoods?

Settlers built Fort Nashborough in 1779 beside the Cumberland. The town was incorporated in 1806, became the state's permanent capital in 1843, and a Metro charter joined it to the county in 1963. Nashville's public schools date to Hume School in 1855, and the unified Metro district now lists 160 schools, including 12 zoned high schools that run career-focused Academies of Nashville and a set of magnet schools with themes such as arts, languages and sciences. Families moving in often ask whether a house is zoned for a magnet option, and MNPS can answer that for a specific address.

Housing from many eras sits side by side. Sellers of older houses can pull the year built and living area from the Assessor's record and check them against the listing. Roof age, foundation movement and old wiring are the items buyers most often ask about, so price those in or fix them before showings.

What are the quickest ways to sell a Nashville house?

Listing the house draws the biggest crowd of buyers, along with showings, appraisals and repair demands. Selling to a cash buyer who takes the house in its current state gives up some of that reach for speed, because closing waits on title work rather than a lender.

Whichever you choose, get the price in writing, state in the contract who pays the recording tax, and have a title company prepare and file the deed. Deal with liens, back taxes and any rental permit questions before closing day.

More questions about Nashville, TN

Will I owe Davidson County tax if I sell in November?

Yes, for the months you owned it. The bill covers all of the calendar year, and the settlement statement should split it between you and the buyer.

Can a Nashville owner contest the tax rate?

No. The Assessor says only values can be appealed, and the Mayor and Metro Council set the rate. The 2025 figures were $2.814 and $2.782 for the two service districts.

How much does the state charge to record a Nashville deed?

The transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of price, and the state recording fee has a $10 minimum. The Register of Deeds has an online calculator for exact totals.

Can a buyer take over my short term rental permit?

No. Metro Codes bars assignment to another person, entity or address, and a change of ownership cancels the permit. The new owner must apply again.

Where can I pay Metro property tax in person?

At the Trustee's office, Suite 220 of the Howard Office Building, 700 President Ronald Reagan Way. Hours are weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.

What should I know before selling a house in Memphis?

Memphis is a large, river-based city, and a sale here is shaped by Shelby County offices more than by city hall alone. The county assessor values the property, the Board of Equalization hears value disputes, and the Register of Deeds records the deed. Knowing which office handles which step keeps a fast sale from stalling.

Census Bureau figures for mid-2025 show 609,647 people, about 3 percent fewer than the April 2020 base. Memphis spreads over roughly 297 square miles, and the median home value of $169,000 is a citywide figure. Price your expectations against your own street and the condition of your house.

How did the city's layout and economy come about?

Memphis sits on the Chickasaw Bluffs above the Mississippi River. John Overton, James Winchester and Andrew Jackson founded the modern city in 1819, and river trade and cotton built its early wealth. Today the largest employer is FedEx, whose global air hub operates at Memphis International Airport, and the Port of Memphis ranks as the fifth-busiest inland water port in the country.

Interstate 40 and Interstate 55 cross the Mississippi here, which is why logistics and warehousing dominate the job market. Census figures show the transportation and warehousing sector alone took in about $10.7 billion in receipts in 2022.

Memphis-Shelby County Schools serves the city, and the University of Memphis, LeMoyne-Owen College and Rhodes College are its main colleges. Overton Park in Midtown and the 4,500-acre Shelby Farms are the two large green spaces buyers mention most.

Owners live in fewer than half of Memphis homes, so rentals make up a large part of the housing stock. If tenants live in your house, give any buyer the lease terms and dates up front.

How does Memphis weather affect an older house?

The Memphis climate is hot and humid in summer. The city averages about 55 inches of rain a year and roughly 64 days above 90 degrees. Severe thunderstorms arrive mostly in spring, with hail, strong wind, flooding and the occasional tornado, and ice storms can bring tree limbs down onto roofs and power lines.

  • Roofs and gutters take the most wear from storms and heat, so check for missing shingles and sagging gutters.
  • Tree limbs over a roofline can come down in an ice storm.
  • Air conditioning age matters, since the summers are long and humid.

A buyer paying cash will usually price these items in and skip the repair negotiation. A buyer using a mortgage may ask for a roof or HVAC credit after the inspection.

How are Memphis property taxes billed and paid?

Memphis sends its own city bill, apart from the one Shelby County issues. The City Council fixes the rate in June, and anything unpaid after August 31 becomes delinquent and grows by 1.5 percent each month. Values come from the Shelby County Assessor's roll as it stood on January 1.

Extra charges can ride along on the city bill: grass cutting, demolition and board-up, new sidewalk work and anti-neglect fees. Before listing, ask the City Treasury at 125 North Main Street for the current statement, since a closing agent will want every line cleared.

  • Owners 65 or older may qualify for the Tax Relief or Tax Freeze programs, both tied to income limits that the state resets yearly.
  • A Quarterly Payment Program lets homeowners 65 and up split the year into four equal parts, due August 31, November 30, February 28 and May 31.
  • Real estate taxes that remain unpaid after a full year go to delinquent tax attorneys the next February 1.

The county bill follows a different calendar. The Tennessee Comptroller's schedule makes county tax payable the first Monday of October, interest-free through February 28 and delinquent on March 1. Residential parcels are assessed at one quarter of appraised value.

Can I appeal my Memphis assessment, and when?

You could have, and the filing period has ended. The Shelby County Board of Equalization took challenges to 2025 values between May 1 and June 30, 2026. A value left unchallenged by then generally stands for the year, so phone the Board at (901) 222-7300 to learn when the next period opens.

Filing costs nothing. The Board's online eFile site only runs during appeal season, hearing notices go out two or more weeks ahead, and every exhibit has to be brought to the hearing itself. Results vary: a hearing can lower the value, raise it or leave it alone.

An easier first step is the Assessor's informal review. It is not a formal appeal, though the office says it clears up many disagreements. Helpful backup includes closed sales of comparable houses nearby, a recent private appraisal and dated photos of the property's condition. The Assessor's Action Center answers at 901-222-7001.

What happens at the Shelby County Register of Deeds when I sell?

Your deed is filed at the Register of Deeds office on Mullins Station Road (Building W-3, in the 38134 area of the city). By the office's own account, a recorded deed is typically back in the mail within a single business day, and a scanned image goes online. People who hold an e-file account can submit documents without a visit.

Recording triggers Tennessee's realty transfer tax, which the Department of Revenue prices at 37 cents for every $100 of the larger of sale price or fair value. Whoever receives the property, the grantee, owes that tax, and the grantee has to state the true consideration under oath on the instrument before the clerk will accept it.

Register's staff only record. They are barred from giving legal advice or helping with form wording, so lean on a closing attorney or title agent for the deed itself. If you need your earlier deed or a trust deed release, the office will find it and certify a copy.

Do short-term rental rules matter if I sell a Memphis house?

They can. Properties used as short-term rentals in Memphis must be registered through the Short-term Rental Registry kept by the Memphis and Shelby County Division of Planning and Development. A business in the city also needs both a City of Memphis and a Shelby County license, at $15 each. If you operate a rental out of the house you are selling, tell the buyer which registration it holds and gather the paperwork.

Ask the Division of Planning and Development for current fees and any pending changes before you list, since the City Council has been working on enforcement language for short-term rentals.

More questions about Memphis, TN

Who owes the transfer tax on a Memphis home sale?

The buyer owes it, as the person receiving title. The state charges 37 cents per $100 of the larger of price or value, and the Shelby County register takes payment at recording. Your contract may allocate it differently, so read that clause.

Is the Memphis assessment appeal window still open?

No. The Board of Equalization took appeals of 2025 assessments from May 1 through June 30, 2026. Call (901) 222-7300 for the next window, and use the Assessor's informal review at 901-222-7001 in the meantime.

What happens if I owe back city taxes on a Memphis house?

They accrue interest at 1.5 percent a month after August 31, and real estate taxes unpaid for a full year go to delinquent tax attorneys on the next February 1. Back taxes, plus any weed cutting or demolition charges on the bill, are normally settled out of your payout when the sale closes.

How quickly does Shelby County record a deed?

Within about one business day, according to the Register of Deeds, which mails the deed back and posts an image online. E-file account holders can send documents electronically.

Can a Memphis homeowner over 65 get property tax help?

Yes. The City offers a Tax Relief Program, a Tax Freeze Program and a Quarterly Payment Program for qualifying owners 65 or older, with the first two tied to state income limits. Contact the City Treasury at 901-522-1111 to apply.

Which selling route fits a Knoxville house best?

Knoxville owners choose between an agent listing, a sale without an agent, and a purchaser paying cash for the home as it stands. The right route depends on repairs, timing and what the house is worth to an ordinary buyer.

Census QuickFacts lists 202,021 residents for July 1, 2025, a 6.0% gain on the 2020 base. Owners occupy only 46.6% of Knoxville housing, and the 2020-2024 median value for those homes is $239,700. Landlords and heirs holding a second house are therefore a big share of local sellers.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, plus showings, repair requests after the buyer's inspection and carrying costs while you wait.
  • Sale without an agent: you keep the commission and take on the contract, the deed and closing coordination.
  • Cash purchase: no showings, a closing date you choose, and a price that reflects the repairs the buyer absorbs.

How do the parts of Knoxville differ for a seller?

Knoxville stretches over roughly 104 square miles along the Tennessee River in the Great Appalachian Valley, according to Wikipedia. Buyers sort the city into five areas, and each pulls a different kind of house.

  • Downtown and the Old City: mixed residential and commercial blocks around Gay Street, next to the University of Tennessee campus and Fort Sanders.
  • South Knoxville: across the river, with Vestal, Island Home Park and Colonial Hills, served by Chapman Highway and Alcoa Highway.
  • West Knoxville: Sequoyah Hills, Bearden, Cedar Bluff and the Kingston Pike corridor near West Town Mall and Turkey Creek.
  • East Knoxville: Parkridge, Burlington, Morningside and Five Points along Magnolia Avenue.
  • North Knoxville: Fountain City and Inskip-Norwood, with Broadway as the commercial spine.

Interstates 40 and 75 meet west of downtown, I-640 bypasses the north side, and I-140 (Pellissippi Parkway) links West Knoxville with McGhee Tyson Airport and Maryville. Census figures show a 20.2-minute average commute for Knoxville workers, and the metro area holds about 958,000 people.

Do Knoxville weather and hills change what a house is worth?

They can, through heat, rain and slope. Summers in Knoxville run hot and wet: the city averages 36 days at 90 degrees or above, rain and melted snow totaling just under 52 inches in a year, and about 4.6 inches of actual snowfall, per the Wikipedia climate summary.

Ridges such as Sharp's Ridge, Brown Mountain and Beaver Ridge mean many lots slope, and First, Second and Third Creek cut through older neighborhoods. Inspectors tend to start with drainage, crawl space moisture, roof age and cooling equipment. Owners who would rather skip that work sometimes prefer an as-is buyer.

What do Knoxville city and Knox County tax bills mean for a seller?

A house inside the city receives two bills, one from the City of Knoxville and one from Knox County, and an unpaid balance on either follows the property to its next owner. The city's property tax page warns that a seller's promise to pay does not change what the city may collect from the buyer.

The county assessor sets values, and that office answers at 865-215-2360. The city revenue office at 865-215-2084 can produce a bill for a property when a buyer asks for one. Closing agents divide the tax year between the two parties, so request the proration sheet before you sign.

Can I sell a Knoxville house that was a short-term rental?

You can sell it, and the sale needs no city approval, but ask the Business Tax Office how a permit is handled when ownership changes. The city requires a permit for any stay under 30 days, and its ordinance has applied since January 2018, per the short-term rental page.

  • Type 1 permits cover owner-occupied homes in residential areas.
  • Type 2 permits cover non-owner-occupied units in non-residential areas.
  • Applications and yearly renewals go through the Business Tax Office.
  • The city pays Host Compliance to match online listings against permits, and unpermitted owners can be cited.

A 24-hour complaint line (865-337-8275) is part of that program, which is another reason to settle permit status before you list.

Which permits and records can slow a Knoxville closing?

Open or missing building permits are the records most likely to hold up a Knoxville deal. The city runs permits through its Plans Review and Inspections portal, with separate tracks for single-family and townhouse construction, mechanical, electrical and plumbing work, and home occupations.

The Knox County Property Assessor looks at each property every other year and also checks permit progress, so a remodel or addition can change the appraised value. If you added a room, you can ask the assessor for a field review so the record matches the house. The assessor says a new owner's name shows up in its system about a week after the deed is filed, and the state requires a sales questionnaire whenever title changes hands.

How is a Knoxville deed recorded?

The signed deed goes to the Knox County Register of Deeds in Suite 225 of the City County Building, 400 Main Street. Staff there say most documents are recorded the day they arrive, that signatures need a notary or two witnesses, and that no deadline exists for recording, though delay can cause legal trouble. The details are in the office's FAQ.

Tennessee's state transfer tax is 37 cents on every $100 of the sale price, per state revenue officials, so a $240,000 sale carries $888. The Register records documents but cannot draft a deed or give legal advice, and a certified copy of a lost deed costs $1.00 a page. The county also offers a free email alert when a document is recorded under your name.

What tax help exists for older or disabled Knoxville homeowners?

The Knox County Trustee runs two programs for people who live in the home they own, and both need a new application every year. The Trustee's page gives these 2026 figures.

  • Elderly or disabled homeowner relief: a state-funded credit of up to $85, with a combined 2025 income limit of $38,470.
  • Veterans with a total service-connected disability and their widows or widowers: up to $444, with no income cap.
  • Senior tax freeze: open at age 65 and over with combined income below $63,470, covering a single home and up to five acres.

Relief is a payment credit and not an exemption, so the bill still arrives. Selling mid-year? Ask the Trustee how the credit is treated before closing.

More questions about Knoxville, TN

Do repairs have to be done before a Knoxville sale?

No, repairs are your decision. An as-is purchase folds the needed work into the offer price, whereas a listing invites inspection requests.

Who is responsible for unpaid Knoxville property tax after a sale?

The new owner inherits it. Per the City of Knoxville, delinquent tax stays with the parcel regardless of what the contract says, so call the Revenue Office and clear old balances first.

How soon can a Knoxville sale close?

It depends mostly on title work and on whether the buyer needs a loan. Once closing is done, the Register of Deeds says documents are generally recorded the day they arrive.

Can heirs sell a house they inherited in Knoxville?

Yes, once the person with authority over the estate can sign the deed. The Register of Deeds explains that a death can change ownership without a new deed when the right wording and a death certificate are recorded, so ask the title company or a probate attorney what your case needs.

What are the Knox County recording costs?

Tennessee statute sets the recording fee, and the state transfer tax adds 37 cents on every $100 of price. Call the Register of Deeds at 865-215-2330 for the fee on your particular document.

King and Stringer's Ridge. Ask the Land Development Office whether a local district covers your address before you promise a buyer any exterior renovation.

Public schools fall under Hamilton County Schools, formed in the 1997 merger of the city and county systems. Ask your listing agent or buyer which zone a given address falls in before quoting school information.

Yes, mainly through flooding history, tornado risk and heat. The river's worst flood came in 1867, and the Tennessee Valley Authority reservoir system created after 1933 now regulates it; the highest stage since then, about 37 feet, came in 1973. The climate adds 52 days a year of 90-degree weather or hotter and more than 52 inches of annual precipitation.

Tornadoes have hit the area too. An EF3 tornado struck southeastern Chattanooga on the night of April 12, 2020. Inspectors working for buyers check roof condition, tree cover and drainage, and a seller who has fixed those items in advance gets a cleaner negotiation.

Hilly lots bring their own checks, and a seller can prepare a short file for them:

  • Engineer letters on foundations built on sloped ground.

Keep that file ready so it can go out with the first offer.

Notices go out in September, taxes are due October 1, and payment stays penalty-free until February's final day. From March 1, interest and penalty total 1.5 percent a month. Prior-year delinquent taxes are filed in Hamilton County Chancery Court each March, and the city says a property can be sold after three years of delinquency.

Homeowners 65 or older can apply for the city's Tax Freeze, which holds the city portion of the bill steady for one year. The application page sets a combined 2025 income limit of $63,470 and says the home must be the primary residence. The 2026 application deadline is April 5, 2027.

The freeze covers city taxes only. County taxes and fees such as stormwater are not frozen, and the owner has to reapply every year or the taxes revert to the current rate and value. Applicants submit proof of ownership, residency, age and income, and the Senior Programs line is 423-643-7274.

Until closing day, keep the application current, since a lapse returns your city bill to the current rate and value.

Request an informal review from the Hamilton County Assessor of Property first. Phone the Assessor at 423-209-7300, weekdays between 8 and 4:30, to ask about the next cycle. The city's tax page says properties are reappraised every four years and that the equalization board at the county takes appeals when the informal review fails, reached at the same number.

After a denial at the county level, the state's appeal guide allows a filing until August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the local notice, whichever is later.

Does Chattanooga let me host short-term guests before I sell?

Only with a city certificate, and the zoning rules are tight. The Short-Term Vacation Rental page says every host needs a certificate. A homestay is owner-occupied for at least 183 days a year and costs $250 to apply or renew. An absentee rental costs $500 and is allowed only in commercial zones C-C, C-R, C-MU1 and C-MU2 and form-based zones CC, CX, IX, RF, RV and SH.

Certificates last one year and the Board of Zoning Appeals cannot exceed the 25 percent density cap. Applications have a 60-day life from submission, and a rezoned property cannot get an absentee certificate for 18 months. For a seller, the useful rule is that a valid certificate can be transferred to a new owner of the same address, though the occupancy type cannot change. Call the Land Development Office at 423-643-5891 with questions.

Where do Chattanooga deeds get filed and what does the state charge?

Register Marc Gravitt's office, in the courthouse at 625 Georgia Avenue (Room 400), takes Chattanooga deeds at 423-209-6560 on weekdays from 8 until 4. Its stated duty is to record deeds and similar instruments and to collect the fees and taxes attached to them.

The state's realty transfer tax is 37 cents per $100 of price, which makes about $1,048 on a $283,200 sale. A separate mortgage tax of 11.5 cents per $100 applies to borrowed amounts above the first $2,000. Request the full cost list from the title company before the closing date.

Closing is possible within about two weeks when title is clear and any estate or lien paperwork is ready. The Hamilton County Register of Deeds files the deed after signing. Delays usually come from payoff letters and co-owner signatures.

What is the Chattanooga city property tax rate?

The city's tax page lists $1.93 per hundred dollars of assessed value, with homes assessed at 25 percent of appraisal. Hamilton County tax is separate, so ask the Trustee at 423-209-7270 for the county rate.

Who covers the state transfer tax on a Chattanooga sale?

The rate is 37 cents per $100 of price, collected at recording. Your purchase contract says who is responsible, and the title company shows the amount on the closing statement.

Does a vacation rental certificate pass to a buyer?

Yes. It can move to the new owner of the same property when the buyer files the transfer application. It cannot follow the operator to a different address, and the occupancy type stays the same.

When does Hamilton County reappraise next?

The city's tax page says properties are reappraised every four years. Call the Hamilton County Assessor at 423-209-7300 for the next effective date.

The county assessor, at 615-790-5708, handles questions about assessed value and the mailing address on a bill.

Recording also triggers state tax. Revenue Department rates apply to the paperwork: 37 cents for every $100 of the sale price as realty transfer tax, and 11.5 cents per $100 of a buyer's loan above the first $2,000 as mortgage tax. The register collects both and sends them on to the state.

Whoever the contract names. The rate is $0.37 per $100 of price, paid when the deed is recorded in Gallatin, and the settlement statement shows the amount.

The Sumner County Register of Deeds, 355 N. Belvedere Drive, Suite 201, Gallatin, 615-452-3892. Title companies normally submit electronically.

When is the next Sumner County reappraisal?

2029, according to the assessor. The most recent reflected values as of January 1, 2024, and yearly appeals go to the county Board of Equalization beginning June 1.

Are weekend rentals allowed in Hendersonville?

Only in Old Town Commercial and General Commercial zones, with a site plan, use and occupancy permit and business license. Rentals of 30 days or longer fall outside the short-term rule.

The notice follows the January 1 owner. If you sell in the fall, the bill still arrives in your name, so the closing statement has to divide the year with the buyer. Have the title company work out the split and check the Trustee's record before closing.

Start with the county Assessor of Property, then take the matter to the equalization board, which sits in June. Five residents serve on that board, appointed by the County Commission for two-year terms.

The assessor's office phone is 615-790-5708. An informal conversation often clears up a factual error, such as wrong square footage, but it does not replace the board appointment. Skipping that hearing can end the appeal, since the state's value appeals page says a disputed assessment generally has to be heard locally first.

A state filing is due on August 1 of the tax year, or 45 days after the local notice went out, whichever comes later. For residential property, the state says the best evidence is sales of comparable homes, with adjustments for size, age, condition and location. An appraisal can be used too.

Generally no, if the house sits in a single-family district. The city's short-term rental page says the municipal code bars stays under three months in those districts, citing Section 78-19(e), and reports citations against owners who kept renting after a warning.

That matters to a seller who hoped to cover carrying costs with Airbnb income while a house sits on the market. Buyers and their lenders also tend to read recent citations as a red flag.

The Department of Revenue sets the state realty transfer tax at 37 cents for every $100 of price. A $1,031,300 sale, matching the Census value for a Brentwood owned home, would owe about $3,816.

A separate mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 applies to debt secured by a recorded deed of trust, with the first $2,000 exempt. Your title company handles both calculations and the filing.   • Confirm every owner on the deed will sign before a notary.

  • An as-is cash purchase: the buyer inspects, makes an offer, and closes on the date you pick. You skip repairs, showings and lender conditions.
  • A pre-listing renovation: you fix the roof, drainage and mechanical items, then list at full market value. This returns more money but takes months and cash up front.
  • A direct sale to a neighbor or relative: workable when both sides have financing lined up and agree on a price.

Ask any buyer for the proof of funds, the closing date in writing, and the title company that will handle the closing. Compare the net figure after taxes, payoff and recording, not the headline number.

The timeline depends on payoff letters, any estate paperwork and how fast the Williamson County Register of Deeds can record the deed. Occupied or inherited houses usually need extra days for title review.

Do I still owe property tax after selling a Brentwood house?

You owe tax for the months you held the house, and the closing statement normally splits the year. The county bill goes to whoever held title on January 1. The Williamson County Trustee at 615-790-5709 can confirm whether the current year is paid.

What is the Brentwood city property tax rate?

The county's 2026 table lists 19 cents for each $100 of assessed value, added to the $1.30 county rate, for $1.49 together. Homes are assessed at 25 percent of appraisal. The Trustee can confirm the amount on your own bill, since relief programs change it.

Can I put my Brentwood home on a short-term rental site while I wait to sell?

Not in a single-family district for stays under three months. The city's municipal code, Section 78-19(e), prohibits it, and the planning page notes past citations. Call Planning and Codes at 615-371-2204 before renting.

Which office records a Brentwood deed?

The Williamson County Register of Deeds in Franklin takes it, and Brentwood City Hall does not. The office is at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, phone 615-790-5706. The state's transfer tax of 37 cents per $100 of price is collected at recording.

With 2,068 residents per square mile and a shrinking head count, Germantown is a city where houses change hands one at a time rather than in big new subdivisions.

What do Census numbers show for Germantown homes?

Germantown is a city of homeowners. QuickFacts lists an owner-occupied rate of 86.7 percent, well above Franklin at 63.8 percent and Gallatin at 57.1 percent, with 15,568 households and 2.60 people per household. The median home value is $470,800 for 2020 to 2024. Median owner costs are $2,546 a month with a mortgage and $923 without one, and median gross rent is $1,816.

Median household income is $149,920, and 71.9 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Residents 65 and older make up 24.2 percent of the population, and 92.3 percent lived in the same house one year earlier.

Which school systems serve Germantown houses?

  • Shelby County Schools: Germantown Elementary, Germantown Middle and Germantown High, an International Baccalaureate school
  • Private options: Evangelical Christian School, St. George's Independent School, The Bodine School, Our Lady of Perpetual Help and others

Because the two systems overlap, a seller should confirm the zoned school with the district before putting a line about it in a listing.

What does Germantown property tax cost and when is it due?

The city rate is $1.7825 per $100 of assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, commercial at 40 percent and personal property at 30 percent. Shelby County sets its own appeal path. A request for an informal review at the assessor's office closes on the last day of May. The county Board of Equalization takes appeals from May 1 through June 30 with no filing fee, online or by mail, and a later step goes to the State Board of Equalization and then Shelby County Chancery Court. The 2026 filing window closed on June 30, 2026, and the board's page says it opens again each May 1.

What do code compliance and permits mean for a Germantown sale?

The Economic and Community Development Department, at 1920 S. Germantown Road, runs planning, public art and code compliance. Its Code Compliance officers enforce the Code of Ordinances, and staff there also support the Planning, Design Review, Public Art and Economic Development commissions and the Board of Zoning Appeals. Three city resources matter most to a seller:

  • A residential ordinance guide covering noise, parking, pet ownership and signage
  • Property maintenance standards for landscaping, trash disposal, exterior upkeep and nuisance prevention
  • Project guidelines and permit information for additions, fences and similar improvements

Before listing, call Code Compliance at 901-757-7281 and ask whether any open case is attached to the address. A sale can go smoothly or stall on that single question, and a seller who knows the answer can price the house with it in mind.

How is a Germantown deed recorded in Shelby County?

Germantown deeds are recorded by the Shelby County Register of Deeds, 1075 Mullins Station Road, Suite W165, Memphis, phone 901-222-8100. The office says a deed is usually recorded and mailed back in about one business day, with a digital copy online. Individuals cannot open an e-filing account on their own, and the office recommends a real estate professional who already has one. A quit claim deed typically costs about $12 to file.

If an owner has died without a probated will, the register notes that Tennessee requires one Affidavit of Heirship filed with its office, and that title companies often prefer three. Probate questions go to the Shelby County Probate Court Clerk at 901-222-3750.

The state's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, paid by the grantee at recording, and the register collects it for the Department of Revenue.

What share of Germantown homes are owner-occupied?

About 86.7 percent, according to Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024. The median owner-occupied home value is $470,800.

Who records a deed for a Germantown house?

The Shelby County Register of Deeds in Memphis records it. Call 901-222-8100, and expect the document back in about one business day.

At about 1,100 feet, Cookeville sits a few hundred feet above Nashville and Knoxville, so heat and humidity run slightly lower. It lies near the crossroads of Interstate 40, State Route 136 and U.S. 70N, roughly 79 miles east of Nashville and 101 miles west of Knoxville.

Tennessee Tech University has been in Cookeville since 1915 and anchors the housing demand near Willow Avenue. Putnam County Schools, with Cookeville High School among the state's larger high schools, is a major employer as well.

Where did Cookeville start, and does the history matter to a seller?

Cookeville takes its name from Richard Fielding Cooke, who settled in the area in 1810 and later served in the state senate. Putnam County was formed in 1842 and re-established in 1854, when state law required a county seat. Land bought by Charles Crook became that seat because natural springs could support a town.

The terrain explains why. Two bills arrive. The Putnam County Trustee collects county tax only, and the City of Cookeville collects its own tax at City Hall, 45 E Broad Street. The trustee reports a 2025 county rate of $2.66 per $100 of assessed value, which the County Commission sets, usually in July.

The county's payment window opens the first Monday of October and closes with the last day of February. March 1 starts interest at 1.5% a month, and anything still owed goes to Chancery Court on March 31. The Clerk and Master then collects delinquent county taxes and runs tax sales. The city follows a similar calendar: its notice for 2023 taxes set a 4:30 p.m. deadline on March 31, 2025, with no postmarks accepted, after which the Clerk and Master took over collection.

The trustee's page says taxes are typically prorated at closing and that the office does not do the proration, so rely on your closing company. The county trustee's number is 931-526-8845, and the Cookeville property tax office is at 931-520-5250.

Can older or disabled Cookeville owners get property tax relief?

Yes. The state repays part of the tax for qualifying homeowners, and Putnam County describes three tracks on its Trustee page.

  • Elderly or disabled homeowners: age 65 by December 31, or totally and permanently disabled, with combined income under $38,470.
  • Tax freeze: age 65 or older with household income at or below $42,200.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses who meet the listed disability categories.

Relief applies only to a primary residence and is a state payment, not an exemption. Recipients must pay in the office or by mail, since banks cannot take relief payments. If you are selling a home you have been getting relief on, ask the trustee how the sale affects your application.

What happens to the deed when a Cookeville house sells?

The Putnam County Register of Deeds records the new deed. State recordation tax combines a realty transfer tax with a mortgage tax, and the revenue department explains on its recordation tax page that the register collects both and sends the money to the state.

Ask the Putnam County Register of Deeds for the present recording fee and any document requirements. When a house has been inherited or has multiple owners, have the closing company confirm who must sign. The Clerk and Master's office in Chancery Court handles matters such as partition and quiet title, which can arise when ownership is unclear.

Can I sell my Cookeville house with tenants still living in it?

Yes. With renters in most Cookeville homes, tenant-occupied sales are common. Give the buyer the lease and deposit details, and ask your closing company how the deposit moves at closing.

When are Putnam County property taxes due?

They are payable from the first Monday in October through the last day of February without interest. Interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1.

Does the county trustee also collect Cookeville city tax?

No. The Putnam County Trustee collects county tax only. City tax is paid at Cookeville City Hall, 45 E Broad Street.

What happens to unpaid Cookeville property tax?

Unpaid county tax goes to Chancery Court on March 31 and the Clerk and Master collects it with added fees and interest. The city sends its own unpaid taxes there too after its deadline.

Who prorates property tax at a Cookeville closing?

Your closing company does. The Putnam County Trustee states it does not prorate taxes between buyers and sellers, so ask your closing agent how the year is split.

Many of the first houses were put up fast from cemesto panels, which are bonded cement and asbestos, so an inspector or buyer may ask about the original construction of an older house here.

Two. Statements go to whatever owner address the state held on January 1. After a spring or summer sale, the new owner may never receive one, and the city says closing normally covers that gap. Chapter 5 of Title 13 allows residential rental inspection districts, so a landlord with a rental to sell should ask Planning and Development whether the address is in one. See the city's Codes Enforcement page.

Check which county holds your parcel before ordering a title search, because Anderson and Roane keep separate records and tax maps. Most sellers leave the search and filing to the title company.

Many homes sit on the steep northeastern slope of Blackoak Ridge, and the east-side lakefront has trails and picnic areas, so lot shape and slope matter more here than in a flat grid. Where is Farragut, Tennessee, and who lives there?

Farragut is a suburban town in Knox County with a small extension into Loudon County, part of the Knoxville metro area. The Town's own facts page gives its size as 16.2 square miles. Interstate 40/75 forms most of the northern edge, Turkey Creek Road and the Norfolk Southern rail line mark the south, the Loudon County line is the west boundary, and Lovell Road plus the Concord Hills subdivisions close off the east.

The 2020 census counted 23,506 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 25,121, a gain of 6.9 percent. Median age in 2020 was 46.7, and 23.7 percent of people were 65 or older. Married couples headed 70.8 percent of the 8,521 households. Of 8,992 housing units, 5.2 percent sat vacant, with a 1.5 percent vacancy rate among owner homes and 14.3 percent among rentals.

Those figures come from the census and the Town's facts page, and they are a useful backdrop for anyone weighing a sale of a Farragut house.

How did Farragut become a town?

The area began as Campbell's Station, a fort and stagecoach stop built by Captain David Campbell in 1787. The brick Campbell's Station Inn went up in 1810 and still stands on Kingston Pike within sight of Town Hall. The Battle of Campbell's Station was fought here on November 16, 1863. The town takes its name from Union Admiral David Farragut, who was born just east of here in 1801.

Incorporation came late. In December 1979 the Knoxville City Council voted to annex stretches of I-40 right-of-way in the Farragut area, and residents petitioned for an incorporation election. Farragut voted to incorporate on January 16, 1980, which blocked further annexation by Knoxville. Bob Leonard was elected the first mayor on April 1, 1980.

What does the land and climate mean for a Farragut house?

Farragut sits in hilly ground between Blackoak Ridge to the north and Fort Loudoun Lake on the Tennessee River to the south, at about 936 feet above sea level. Hills mean sloped lots, and sloped lots mean buyers and inspectors pay attention to drainage, retaining walls and foundations.

The Town reports these climate averages:

  • Annual precipitation of 47.86 inches and about 6 inches of snow
  • January highs near 46 degrees and July highs near 88
  • A freeze-free period averaging 214 days
  • Prevailing winds from the southwest

Nearly 48 inches of rain a year puts roofs, gutters and crawl spaces on every inspection list. A seller who has patched a leak or regraded a yard should keep the receipts for the buyer.

What does property tax look like for a Farragut homeowner?

Farragut levies no municipal property tax. Residents pay Knox County's rate of $1.55 per $100 of assessed value, and the Town reports that residential property is assessed at 25 percent of market value and commercial at 40 percent. Knox County sales tax is 9.25 percent, or 5.25 percent on groceries.

For a house valued at $600,000, the assessed value would be $150,000, and $1.55 per $100 yields $2,325 a year. That sum is an illustration built from the published rate, so check the actual bill on the trustee's site.

The Knox County Property Assessor reappraises on a two-year schedule and mails a notice whenever an assessed value changes. An owner who disagrees can appeal to the County Board of Equalization when it meets in June. The assessor also says that after a deed is recorded, its system can take up to a week to show the new owner.

Which permits and code rules affect a Farragut sale?

Farragut's Building and Fire Codes Division enforces the adopted building, plumbing, gas, mechanical, housing, swimming pool and fire codes. A permit is needed for most remodeling. Water heater change-outs, HVAC replacements and any gas appliance installation require permits and inspections through the Town, and mechanical applications must include a Manual J report. Electrical inspections run through the Lenoir City Utilities Board.

Work that skips a permit is the usual snag at closing, so it helps to confirm what was permitted before listing. Items on the Town's no-permit list include one-story detached sheds up to 200 square feet and fences up to 7 feet, though zoning approval may still apply.

Code enforcement follows a set path:

  • A complaint is reviewed and an officer does a drive-by inspection.
  • A courtesy notice goes to the owner, usually with a 10-day deadline, though it can range from immediate to 30 days.
  • If the problem persists, the owner can be cited to Municipal Court, where fines reach $50 per day per violation.
  • The Town may fix the problem itself and place a lien on the property for the cost.

A seller with an open notice should call Town Hall at 865-966-7057 before accepting any offer, because a lien would have to be dealt with at closing.

Which schools and roads shape demand in Farragut?

Most Farragut addresses are zoned to Knox County Schools: Farragut Primary (K-2), Farragut Intermediate (3-5), Farragut Middle (6-8) and Farragut High (9-12), with Northshore Elementary also serving the area. Part of the town north of I-75 is zoned for Hardin Valley Middle and Hardin Valley Academy. Knoxville Christian School and Concord Christian School are private options.

Kingston Pike, the merged US 70 and US 11, runs through the middle of town, and I-40/75 runs along its northern edge. The town lists commuting links to Oak Ridge, Knoxville, Maryville, Alcoa and McGhee Tyson Airport, and a commuter lot at Campbell Station Road and Campbell Lakes Drive serves ride sharers. Gas comes from the Knoxville Utilities Board, electricity from the Lenoir City Utility Board, and fire protection is subscription-based through Rural Metro.

A buyer who learns about the Rural Metro subscription early will not be surprised by it at closing.

How does a Farragut house sale move from offer to recorded deed?

An owner can list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or take a cash offer from a company that buys houses as-is. A cash sale suits a house that needs work, carries a code notice, or has a deadline attached. Whatever route is chosen, the deed is recorded in Knox County, not at Town Hall.

The Knox County Register of Deeds says a deed should be recorded as soon as possible, though no statutory time limit exists, and that signatures must be notarized or witnessed by two people. Documents are usually recorded the same day received. Tennessee's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of the purchase price, and the Department of Revenue says the grantee pays it when the deed is recorded.

The assessor will send a sales questionnaire after ownership changes, including a private sale or a transfer into a trust. Sellers should also tell the trustee where to mail later bills. Ask the Knox County Trustee how any current-year balance is handled at closing.

More questions about Farragut, TN

Does Farragut have its own property tax?

No. The Town of Farragut levies no municipal property tax, and residents pay the Knox County rate of $1.55 per $100 of assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of market value.

Where is a Farragut deed recorded?

At the Knox County Register of Deeds in Suite 225 of the City County Building, 400 Main Street, Knoxville. Call 865-215-2330. Each county records only the real estate inside its own borders.

Do I need a permit to replace a water heater in Farragut?

Yes. The Town of Farragut requires a permit and inspection for water heater change-outs, HVAC replacements and gas appliance installations. Contact the Codes office at 865-966-7057 or 865-675-2384 if you are unsure.

What happens if Farragut sends me a code courtesy notice before I sell?

Respond before the deadline, usually 10 days. If the issue is still open at the follow-up inspection, the owner can be cited to Municipal Court, with fines up to $50 per day per violation, and the Town can place a lien after fixing the problem.

Who is the transfer tax paid by on a Farragut sale?

The buyer, as grantee. Tennessee charges $0.37 per $100 of purchase price when the deed is recorded, and the Register of Deeds collects it for the Department of Revenue.
